lesson.title: The Signal That Repeats Itself
lesson.summary: A periodic signal is one whose exact waveform repeats at a fixed time interval, the period, forever, and that regularity is what lets an entire waveform be described with a handful of numbers instead of every point in time.
lesson.body:
A signal x(t) is periodic if there exists some positive number T such that x(t + T) = x(t) for every value of t, not just at one instant but for the signal's entire history and future. The smallest T for which this holds is called the period, and it has units of time (seconds, milliseconds, and so on). Familiar periodic signals include AC household power, the clock signal driving a digital circuit, and the sine or square wave produced by a signal generator. In every case, once you have seen one full period, you have effectively seen the entire signal, because the next period, and the one after that, is an exact copy.

Take standard AC power in most of North America, a sinusoid at 60 Hz. Its period is the reciprocal of its frequency: T = 1/f = 1/60 Hz = 0.01667 s, or 16.67 ms. That means the voltage rises from zero, climbs to its positive peak, falls back through zero, dips to its negative peak, and returns to zero, all within 16.67 milliseconds, and then the exact same sequence happens again, indefinitely, without ever changing shape.

Periodicity is not just a tidy label, it is what makes an entire branch of signal analysis possible. Because a periodic signal's shape recurs exactly every T seconds, it turns out that any periodic signal, no matter how jagged or unusual its shape within one period, can be rebuilt from nothing but a sum of sine and cosine waves at one base frequency and whole-number multiples of it. That base frequency is called the fundamental frequency, and the whole-number multiples are called harmonics, both covered in upcoming chapters, and the decomposition itself is the Fourier series, the capstone of this chapter sequence. None of that machinery applies to a signal that never settles into an exact repeating pattern in the first place, which is exactly the case covered next: the aperiodic signal.
